entityDossier.narrative:
The investigation has two halves that need to be tiered separately, because they are not equally evidenced.

The first half is the independent research. UAP Gerb is a pseudonymous researcher and documentarian who produces multi-hour, heavily sourced video investigations into crash retrieval, reverse-engineering facilities and the contractor and laboratory network around them. His signature thesis is not about craft at all but about legal architecture: that the Department of Energy, not the Pentagon, is the load-bearing custodian, that the Nuclear Emergency Support Team has a classified retrieval mission alongside its public one, and that the Atomic Energy Act of 1954 supplies the classification vehicle by designating recovered material as trans-classified foreign nuclear material, a category that sits outside the reach of the congressional intelligence committees. In his August 2025 Danny Jones Podcast appearance he put it directly: the DOE NEST had authority under the 1954 Atomic Energy Act, which also governs how UFO materials are classified as transclassified foreign nuclear materials. This matters because it is a falsifiable structural claim about statute, not a witness anecdote, and because it explains a specific documented behavior, namely why UAP disclosure amendments keep naming the 1954 Act as an obstacle.

The second, and more consequential, half of the investigation is Gerb's January 2026 attack on the AARO to Oak Ridge to Battelle circuit. As reported by IBTimes UK on January 17, 2026, Gerb alleges that in 2024 AARO contracted Oak Ridge National Laboratory to examine a metallic specimen recovered from private land in Ohio; that AARO subsequently issued a brief statement suggesting the sample was ordinary while the full Oak Ridge analysis was never released; that former AARO director Sean Kirkpatrick left government in December 2023 to become Chief Technology Officer for Defense and Intelligence Programs at Oak Ridge, the same laboratory that received material he had previously decided to send out for analysis; that Oak Ridge subsequently removed the webpage announcing his appointment and that he did not list the position on his public CV; and that former Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence and Security Ronald Moultrie removed his prior Battelle board service from his official biography. The structural point behind the personnel allegations is the one that survives regardless of motive: Oak Ridge is operated by UT-Battelle, a Battelle entity, and Battelle is the same institution that performed the statistical analysis published as Project Blue Book Special Report No. 14 in 1955. The organization that wrote the government's foundational public assessment of the phenomenon in the 1950s operates the laboratory that assessed its recovered material in the 2020s. That is not a coincidence anyone has been asked to explain on the record.

The third half, the one that turns research into leverage, is Burlison. Reports in the research community indicate Burlison invited Gerb to dinner, and by May 2026 Burlison had transmitted to MITRE a document whose enclosure lists more than forty specific requests. The letter instructs MITRE to designate a senior official, issue a preservation hold, provide a records-location index, produce unclassified responsive records in native electronic format with complete metadata within 45 days, identify classified or sponsor-controlled material, and coordinate a classified briefing for cleared committee staff. It asks MITRE to identify all work involving detection, tracking, correlation, characterization, data fusion, anomaly detection or attribution of UAP-related signatures across air, space, maritime, undersea, cyber, electromagnetic, acoustic, radar, optical, infrared, nuclear, biological, chemical or multi-intelligence domains. And it includes the trapdoor clause: if no responsive records exist, MITRE must certify the search methodology, repositories searched, custodians contacted, search terms used, date ranges and the responsible MITRE official who supervised the search. That converts a null answer into an attributable, signed, falsifiable statement by a named person, which is exactly the property that a denial needs in order to become evidence.

The MITRE demand did not arrive alone. Burlison's press release states it builds on his earlier letter to MIT Lincoln Laboratory concerning historical UAP records associated with the Beacon Hill Study and a reel-to-reel recording identified as AF-ATIC-FILM, 03/52. A film reel identified by an Air Technical Intelligence Center designator and a March 1952 date, held at an MIT laboratory rather than at the National Archives, is the single most specific artifact anyone in Congress has publicly named in this line of inquiry.

What the record does not yet contain is any MITRE production. As of the reporting, MITRE has said only that insiders are reviewing archives and that if relevant material is found it will coordinate with the responsible federal agencies. That is a conditional, agency-deferring non-answer, which is the standard posture of a contractor that intends to route any responsive material back through the classification authority that created it.

entityDossier.narrative:
The House's involvement runs on a sixty-year cycle of the same three moves: hearing, denial, statute.

Move one, 1966. On April 5, 1966 the Committee on Armed Services of the House of Representatives, 89th Congress, second session, held a hearing on Unidentified Flying Objects, convened after pressure from House Minority Leader Gerald Ford. The Air Force sent Secretary Harold Brown, and Project Blue Book sent Major Hector Quintanilla, its serving chief, and Dr. J. Allen Hynek, its scientific consultant. Brown put the Air Force position on the record: no evidence that UFOs threatened national security or were extraterrestrial. Hynek used the same hearing to place on the record that the Air Force's practice of assigning conventional explanations to every report was a poverty of hypotheses, and to call for an independent civilian scientific panel. The Air Force's response was to fund the Condon study at the University of Colorado, which is the template: a congressional hearing produces not disclosure but an outsourced study whose public summary can be written to a conclusion. That is exactly what had already been done with Battelle and Special Report No. 14 eleven years earlier.

Move two, 2023 to 2026. On July 26, 2023 the Oversight Committee's Subcommittee on National Security, the Border, and Foreign Affairs, chaired by Rep. Glenn Grothman with Rep. Robert Garcia as ranking member, and driven by Reps. Tim Burchett and Anna Paulina Luna, held the first public hearing to take testimony from military pilots and whistleblowers. Ryan Graves's written statement placed three institutional claims into the record: that UAP in U.S. airspace are grossly underreported; that stigma is itself a national security problem; and that excessive classification is hiding what the government knows, with all UAP video classified secret or above since 2021. Graves also entered a specific, dated, attributable account of information suppression: his advisor Rear Admiral Tim Gallaudet received a classified SIPRNET email in 2015 titled 'Urgent safety of flight issue' attaching the GO FAST video, and the following day the email was removed from Gallaudet's system and from his deputy's, with no one ever discussing it again. Gallaudet's own stated presumption is that the removal was connected to a classified special access program. That single paragraph in a House witness statement is the cleanest documented instance of a UAP record being pulled out of an official system.

By 2025 the House had institutionalized the effort. Chairman James Comer created the Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets and named Luna to chair it, with Rep. Jasmine Crockett as ranking member and Republican members Nancy Mace, Tim Burchett, Lauren Boebert, Eric Burlison, Eli Crane and Brandon Gill, and Democratic members Stephen Lynch, Raja Krishnamoorthi and Dave Min. On September 9, 2025 the task force held a hearing on restoring public trust through UAP transparency and whistleblower protection, taking testimony from Air Force veteran Jeffrey Nuccetelli, Chief Alexandro Wiggins, journalist George Knapp and Air Force veteran Dylan Borland.

Move three, statute. The FY2024 National Defense Authorization Act, Public Law 118-31, sections 1841 through 1843, directed NARA to establish the Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Records Collection and required every federal agency to review, identify and organize its UAP records for transmission to the National Archives by October 20, 2024. The statutory definition of what belongs in the collection is the tell: copies of all Government, Government-provided, or Government-funded records relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena, technologies of unknown origin, and non-human intelligence. Congress wrote non-human intelligence into a records statute. NARA's implementing metadata schema then required a mandatory Special Controls field populated with SAP, SCI, RD/FRD and FGI markings, and required the Department of Energy to be entered as a referral agency whenever a file contains Restricted Data or Formerly Restricted Data. The Archives built its intake to receive special-access and nuclear-classified UAP material before anyone had produced any. Separately, section 1687(b) of the same law made UAP-related independent research and development funding unallowable as an indirect expense on covered contracts unless the material is made available to the congressional defense committees, the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence, the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, and the four congressional leaders. That provision exists because someone in Congress concluded that contractors were charging the taxpayer for UAP work through overhead while reporting nothing.

By 2026 the House had pivoted to attacking the contractor and FFRDC layer directly. Burlison's May 2026 interrogatories to MITRE, and his earlier letter to MIT Lincoln Laboratory, assert that a nonprofit FFRDC cannot become a private vault for federal records. On August 1, 2026 Burlison released, with administration authorization, preliminary implementation guidance for President Trump's directive on nondisclosure agreements binding current and former government employees and contractors with UAP information, and invited anyone who believes the directive applies to them to contact his office. That is a sitting member of the House offering himself as the intake channel for people whose NDAs may have just been waived. Running alongside it, and not through it, the administration began posting declassified interagency UAP files in May 2026 on war.gov/ufo, an executive release track that answers to no congressional deadline.

entityDossier.whatItIs: Project Blue Book Special Report No. 14, formally titled 'Analysis of Reports of Unidentified Aerial Objects,' dated 5 May 1955, is the largest statistical study of UFO reports the U.S. government has ever produced. The analysis was performed under contract by Battelle Memorial Institute of Columbus, Ohio, under a project designation reported as Project STORK, using 3,201 cases with an information cut-off of the end of 1952. It was released publicly on October 25, 1955 through Department of Defense Office of Public Information Release No. 1053-55.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: The gap between what the study found and what the government said it found is the cleanest documented instance of deliberate framing in the entire record, and it is verifiable from two documents that were published together. The press release and Secretary of the Air Force Donald Quarles's accompanying statement told the public that the unknowns amounted to three per cent, a figure drawn from 131 sightings in the first four months of 1955, not from the 3,201-case study sample the report actually analyzed. The report body shows unknowns running far higher, and highest precisely where witness reliability was rated Excellent. The release also declined to name Battelle, describing the analysis only as the work of a private scientific group under the supervision of the Air Technical Intelligence Center at Dayton, Ohio. The full 316-page report was then not distributed, on stated grounds of printing cost, until a private citizen reprinted it. Every element of a concealment operation is present and dated: a suppressed dataset, a substituted statistic, an unnamed contractor, and a restricted distribution.
entityDossier.narrative:
Start with what the report says about itself. Its own Summary states that the special study started in 1953, that to provide the study group with a complete set of files the information cut-off date was established as of the end of 1952, and that in these charts, 3201 cases have been used. It describes a three-part analytic method: a systematic attempt to find distinguishing characteristics in the data, a study of any trend or pattern, and an attempt to determine the probability that any of the UNKNOWNS represented observations of technological developments not known to this country. On the first of these it records a genuinely load-bearing finding: 'The first step in the analysis of the data revealed the existence of certain apparent similarities between cases of objects definitely identified and those not identified. Statistical methods of testing when applied indicated a low probability that these apparent similarities were significant.' Read plainly, Battelle tested whether the unknowns looked like the knowns and found that the resemblance did not hold up. That is the opposite of the conclusion the public was handed. The report then walks it back through re-evaluation, concluding that the probability the unknowns represented unknown technology was very small.

Now the release. Department of Defense Office of Public Information Release No. 1053-55, dated October 25, 1955 and headlined 'AIR FORCE RELEASES STUDY ON UNIDENTIFIED AERIAL OBJECTS', opens with the flat assertion that no evidence of the existence of the popularly-termed flying saucers was found. It attributes the work to a private scientific group under the supervision of the Air Technical Intelligence Center at Dayton, Ohio, and never says the word Battelle. It then executes the substitution: since the instigation of the investigation more than seven years ago, methods and procedures have been so refined that of the 131 sightings reported during the first four months of 1955 only three per cent were listed as unknown. Secretary Quarles then attaches his name to that number: 'On the basis of this study we believe that no objects such as those popularly described as flying saucers have overflown the United States. I feel certain that even the unknown three per cent could have been explained as conventional phenomena or illusions if more complete observational data had been available.' The phrase on the basis of this study is doing enormous work. The study is the 3,201-case Battelle analysis. The three per cent is from a 131-case sample the study did not analyze, collected three years after the study's own cut-off date. The two are welded together in a single sentence and a Cabinet-level official signs it.

The attached Summary makes the substitution visible in its own numbers. For cases received before the end of 1952 it gives Unknown at 9 per cent; for the more recent tranche it gives Unknown at 3 per cent. Neither figure is the rate for the 3,201 cases whose charts and tables make up the report.

The body tells a different story, which is why the body was hard to get. Leon Davidson, a chemical engineer who had worked at Los Alamos Scientific Laboratory and who reprinted the report photographically beginning in 1956, wrote in his publisher's analysis that the key to the answer is contained in Fig. 8 (orig. p. 24) and Tables A1, A2, and A3 (orig. pp. 107 and 108); that Fig. 8 shows Unknown sightings constitute 33.3 per cent of all the object sightings for which the reliability of the sighting is considered Excellent; and that Tables A1 through A3 agree, with the percentage of Unknown sightings not less than about 20 per cent even when sightings of lesser reliability are included. The distribution runs the wrong way for the official framing: the better the witness, the more likely the object stayed unidentified.

Distribution was the second layer of the concealment. Davidson reproduces a letter from Air Force Secretary Donald A. Quarles dated July 5, 1956 stating that it has been estimated that the cost of printing enough copies for distribution to the public through such outlets as libraries and academic institutions would be between $10 and $15 per copy. The 316-page full report was therefore never distributed. The non-availability became a matter of congressional record at the House Subcommittee on Government Information under Rep. John E. Moss on November 15, 1956. Davidson's privately financed edition, reproduced photographically page by page with the main text intact, is why the document exists in public hands at all.

One further anomaly sits in the photographic reproduction. Davidson points to original page 295, where the codes for Final Identification carry typewritten strikeovers: the category originally called Rockets and Missiles in the early analytic work was changed to read Insufficient Information, and the category originally called Electromagnetic Phenomenon was changed to read Unknown. If that reading of the page is correct, then the report's residual category was not an empty bin for the unexplained. It was a renamed bin for a hypothesis.

Battelle is the connective tissue. The same institute later formed UT-Battelle, the operator of Oak Ridge National Laboratory, which per contemporary allegations received AARO's 2024 material analysis work. Battelle is also one of the entities Rep. Burlison named in his May 2026 MITRE interrogatories, alongside Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman, Raytheon, Boeing, General Dynamics, SAIC, Leidos, The Aerospace Corporation, Booz Allen Hamilton, BAE Systems and Bigelow Aerospace. The organization that wrote the government's founding public statistical assessment of the phenomenon has never left the file.

entityDossier.whatItIs: A waived unacknowledged special access program is the most tightly held category in the Department of Defense classification system. Department of Defense training doctrine defines it in one sentence: 'Waived SAPs are unacknowledged SAPs for which the Secretary of Defense has waived applicable reporting requirements under Section 119, Title 10 U.S. Code.' The waiver authority is 10 U.S.C. 119(e), under which the Secretary may withhold specified information from the statutory reports to Congress if he determines that including it would adversely affect national security, and must then provide the information and the justification for the waiver only to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: This is the mechanism. If a legacy recovery and reverse-engineering program exists and has been concealed from Congress, waived SAP status is the lawful instrument by which that concealment is accomplished, and no unlawful act is required to sustain it. The statute permits an entire program's existence, cost, milestones and technology to disappear from the reports Congress wrote to keep itself informed, on the unilateral written determination of a single official. The population read in on the legislative side collapses to eight members and, per DoD policy, their staff directors. Everyone else in Congress, including every member of both intelligence committees who is not chair or ranking, can hold a Top Secret clearance and still be told nothing exists. The system is designed to produce truthful denials from officials who genuinely do not know, which is the precise pathology alleged across every UAP whistleblower account since 2017.
entityDossier.narrative:
The architecture has four layers, and each one narrows the audience.

Layer one is the baseline reporting duty. 10 U.S.C. 119, added by Public Law 100-180 section 1132(a)(1) on December 4, 1987, required the Secretary of Defense to submit to the defense committees an annual report on special access programs by March 1 of each year, setting out the total amount requested for SAPs in the President's budget and, for each SAP, a brief description, its major milestones, its actual cost for each prior fiscal year, and its estimated total cost across the current year, the budget year and four succeeding years. Subsection (b) required a separate annual report by February 1 giving notice and justification for each new SAP designation, with the current total program cost estimate and an identification of existing programs or technologies similar in technology or mission to the one being hidden. Subsection (f), added by Public Law 101-510 section 1482(a)(2) in November 1990, added the hard gate: a special access program may not be initiated until the defense committees are notified and thirty days elapse.

Layer two is the waiver. Subsection (e)(1) provides that the Secretary of Defense may waive any requirement under subsection (a), (b), or (c) that certain information be included in a report under that subsection if the Secretary determines that inclusion of that information in the report would adversely affect the national security, with each waiver made on a case-by-case basis. Subsection (e)(2) then routes the withheld information and the justification jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees. Steven Aftergood of the Federation of American Scientists put the practical result plainly: waived SAPs are exempted by statute (10 USC 119e) from normal congressional notification requirements, and in such cases only eight senior members of the congressional defense committees may be advised of the program.

Layer three is DoD policy, which is more restrictive than the statute. Under the pre-2024 SAP policy framework, only the chair, the ranking minority member and the staff directors of the defense and intelligence committees are authorized access to waived DoD SAPs within their committee's oversight role, absent approval by the Secretary or Deputy Secretary. The currently effective directive, DoD Directive 5205.07, reissued September 12, 2024 and approved by Deputy Secretary of Defense Kathleen H. Hicks, adds a provision that is the operational choke point for whistleblowers: no DoD contractor entity, contractor employee, contractor representative, or consultant will provide SAP material to any members of Congress or their staff without Director, DoD SAPCO approval. The people most likely to hold the evidence are contractors, and the directive forbids them from handing it to Congress without permission from the office that runs the SAP system.

Layer four is the quiet erosion of the reporting baseline itself. The U.S. Code note under section 119 records that for termination, effective December 31, 2021, of the provisions in subsections (a) and (b) requiring submittal of an annual report to Congress, see section 1061 of Public Law 114-328. The annual SAP report and the annual new-SAP notification report, the two instruments the 1987 Congress built, were sunset by a general reporting-requirement cull. And the September 12, 2024 reissuance of DoDD 5205.07 does not define waived SAP anywhere in its glossary. It defines SAP, SAP architecture, SAP umbrella, SAP compartment, SAP sub-compartment, Joint Force Integration SAP and Strategic Enabler SAP. The acknowledged, unacknowledged and waived taxonomy that appears in DoD's own training material has been replaced in the public directive by a vocabulary that does not distinguish between programs Congress is told about and programs it is not. Whether that is reform or relabeling, the public governing document no longer names the category.

The rest of the directive maps the custody chain. All DoD SAPs are assigned to an oversight authority drawn from USD(R&E), USD(A&S), USD(P), USD(I&S) and the Director of the DoD SAP Central Office. The Director of DoD SAPCO reports directly to the Deputy Secretary of Defense, holds delegated Top Secret original classification authority for all DoD SAP information, publishes and maintains the security classification guides for every SAP umbrella, accredits congressional SAP facilities, and maintains records of DoD SAP information provided to Congress. Establishment of new SAP umbrellas and compartments is by exception and requires Secretary or Deputy Secretary approval. The senior governing body, the SAP Oversight Committee, is chaired by the Deputy Secretary of Defense. Approximately 75 to 80 per cent of all DoD SAPs are acquisition SAPs, which is the category that would cover a materials exploitation or reverse-engineering effort.

Congress has attacked the funding side rather than the classification side. FY2024 NDAA section 1687(b) makes independent research and development funding relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena unallowable as an indirect expense on covered contracts unless the material and information is made available to the congressional defense committees, both intelligence committees, and the majority and minority leaders of the Senate and the Speaker and minority leader of the House. That is an admission on the face of the statute that Congress believed UAP work was being charged to the taxpayer through contractor overhead and reported to no one. It is also a route around the waiver, because IR&D allowability is an accounting question, not a classification question.

entityDossier.whatItIs: Americans for Safe Aerospace (ASA) is a military pilot-led 501(c)(3) nonprofit founded in 2023 by Ryan Graves, a former U.S. Navy F/A-18F pilot from strike fighter squadron VFA-11. It operates a confidential intake channel through which military and commercial aircrew report UAP encounters, and it functions as the principal non-governmental witness pipeline into Congress. Headquartered at 1620 I St NW Suite 900, Washington, DC, it describes itself as the world's largest UAP advocacy community and reported more than 30,000 members as of 2026, up from roughly 4,000 at its founding.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: ASA is the institution that solved the collection problem the government created. Because there is no protected, non-stigmatizing reporting route for commercial pilots, and because military witnesses face a confusing internal process, the observational data that would test the phenomenon has never been aggregated by the state. ASA aggregates it privately and then feeds it to Congress, which is why its founder's July 2023 testimony landed as the first public congressional hearing to take military pilot and whistleblower evidence. More importantly for a concealment map, ASA is where several people who were inside the classified system have landed: Jay Stratton, former Director of the UAP Task Force; Christopher Mellon, former Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defense for Intelligence; Rear Admiral Tim Gallaudet, former head of NOAA and Oceanographer of the Navy; and Kirk McConnell, former professional staff of the Senate Armed Services Committee. That roster means ASA holds institutional memory of both the task force that collected the data and the committee staff that wrote the oversight statutes. It is a private organization staffed with the government's own former custodians.
entityDossier.narrative:
ASA's origin is a specific failure of the reporting system. Graves joined the Navy in 2009 and by 2014 was flying with VFA-11 near Virginia Beach when a radar upgrade began producing unknown tracks that were initially dismissed as software glitches and then corroborated on infrared, confirming their physical presence. The sightings became routine enough to appear in daily briefs. The pivotal event was in Warning Area W-72, an exclusive block of airspace ten miles east of Virginia Beach where all traffic enters through a single GPS point at a set altitude. As two jets crossed the threshold one hundred feet apart, one pilot saw a dark gray cube inside a clear sphere, motionless against the wind, fixed directly at the entry point. Both aircraft took evasive action and terminated the mission. The squadron filed a safety report. There was no official acknowledgement and no mechanism to report further sightings. Graves founded ASA to build the mechanism that did not exist.

The organization scaled faster than anyone planned. Its July 18, 2023 launch release for the UAP Witness Campaign stated that more than 30 commercial aircrew and military witnesses had already approached it and that ASA had more than 4,000 members. Eight days later, in written testimony to the House Oversight Subcommittee on National Security, the Border, and Foreign Affairs, Graves reported nearly 5,000 members and more than 30 UAP witnesses being actively worked. By 2026 the public membership figure is over 30,000. The witness profile is itself a finding: the majority are commercial pilots at major airlines, often veterans with decades of experience, and their reports frequently open with an apology, in Graves's phrasing, 'I apologize, I realize this will sound crazy.' They describe objects at altitudes apparently above 40,000 feet, potentially in low earth orbit or in the grey zone below the Karman line, executing right-hand turns, retrograde orbits and j-hooks, with recurring clusters north of Hawaii and in the North Atlantic. They are adamant these are not Starlink flares.

ASA's process is deliberately witness-controlled. A pilot or veteran contacts the organization confidentially with an outline, ASA conducts an interview, brings in an advisor with relevant expertise for evaluation, and only then, and only with the witness's explicit permission, are next steps taken, which can include meetings with congressional staff and Members or with AARO. Most witnesses do not want to speak publicly and fear professional consequences; they want their account added to the data set. That design is a direct response to the retaliation problem that runs through the whole file.

The advisory bench is what makes ASA structurally significant rather than merely large. Its pilots include David Fravor and Alex Dietrich, the first former Navy pilots to meet with Congress about their UAP encounter, plus Michael Greene and Sam Fletcher. Its national security advisors are Jay Stratton, former Director of the UAP Task Force, Christopher Mellon, Rear Admiral Tim Gallaudet, and Kirk McConnell, former professional staff on the Senate Armed Services Committee, which is the committee that wrote the AARO statutes and whose chair and ranking member sit inside the eight-member waived-SAP notification group. Its policy advisors include Susan McCue, former chief of staff to Senator Harry Reid, and Bryan Bender, former defense editor at Politico, plus Mike Gold of the NASA UAP Independent Study Team and David Radzanowski, former CFO and Chief of Staff at NASA. Its science bench includes Avi Loeb of Harvard, Garry Nolan of Stanford, Robin Hanson of George Mason and Ravi Starzl of Carnegie Mellon.

The single most operationally important thing ASA has put on the congressional record came through Gallaudet. Graves testified that while serving as an Admiral with Fleet Forces Command, Gallaudet received a classified SIPRNET email in 2015 from the Operations Commander to all one- and two-star subordinates, titled 'Urgent safety of flight issue', attaching the GO FAST video and raising concerns about multiple near mid-air collisions with UAP in the early warning area off Virginia Beach, with a note that the exercise might be shut down for safety reasons. Gallaudet reviewed it with his deputy. The next day the email was removed from both of their systems, and despite routine in-person meetings with that group, no one ever discussed it again. Gallaudet's stated presumption is that the removal was connected to a classified special access program. That is a flag officer, on the record through a congressional witness, describing the retroactive deletion of a safety-of-flight communication.

Graves also entered two hard data points into the House record: that the UAP Task Force reported in 2021 there had been eleven near misses with UAP, citing the ODNI Preliminary Assessment of June 25, 2021, and that in April 2022 the FAA issued an alert to its operations managers that a commercial aircraft over West Virginia experienced a double attitude and double autopilot failure while flying under a UAP. He also flagged an unexplained reversal by AARO's director, who told Congress he operated only under Title 10 authority and needed Title 50 authorities and access to scientifically calibrated intelligence-community sensors, then indicated in his first public interview shortly before the hearing that he had what he needed.

On policy, ASA endorsed the Safe Airspace for Americans Act, H.R. 6967 in the 118th Congress, which would let civilian pilots report through NASA's Aviation Safety Reporting System with anti-retaliation protection and public release of all reports, a mechanism recommended by the NASA UAP Independent Study Team. ASA's July 2023 release also documents the organization's read of the UAP Disclosure Act of 2023, sponsored by Senators Schumer, Rounds, Rubio, Gillibrand, Young and Heinrich, whose central mechanism was a nine-member civilian Review Board empowered to hold hearings, administer oaths, and subpoena UAP witnesses and documents.

entityDossier.whatItIs: The Committee on Armed Services of the United States Senate, one of the four congressional defense committees named in 10 U.S.C. 119(g), and therefore one of the bodies whose chairman and ranking minority member sit inside the eight-member group that may be advised of a waived special access program. SASC is also the drafting venue for the annual National Defense Authorization Act provisions that created the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office, defined unidentified anomalous phenomena in statute, and progressively tightened the reporting obligations attached to them.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: SASC occupies the structural pinch point: it is simultaneously the committee that is supposed to receive notification of the most closely held programs and the committee that keeps writing new statutes because it apparently is not receiving it. The language it has enacted is an admission. 50 U.S.C. 3373(j) requires AARO's historical record report to itemize any program or activity that was protected by restricted access that has not been explicitly and clearly reported to Congress, and any efforts to obfuscate, manipulate public opinion, hide, or otherwise provide incorrect unclassified or classified information about UAP. Congress does not write that sentence about a subject on which it believes it has been told the truth. Subsection (l)(4) goes further, requiring the AARO Director to hand the SASC and SSCI chair and ranking member an enumeration of every instance in which UAP data was withheld from AARO because of classification restrictions or for any other reason, which is a statutory acknowledgment that data is being withheld from the office created to collect it. And in December 2025 Congress had to amend the statute again to extend the immediate data-availability requirement beyond intelligence community elements to Department of Defense components, meaning that for three years the mandate did not reach the department that owns the special access program system.
entityDossier.narrative:
Follow the statutory ratchet, because it is a record of what did not work.

In December 2021, section 1683 of the FY2022 NDAA, Public Law 117-81, 135 Stat. 2118, created the office structure and authorities to address what were then called unidentified aerial phenomena. Twelve months later, in December 2022, Public Law 117-263 rewrote the section twice over: section 1673(c) of the NDAA substituted anomalous for aerial throughout and added congressional leadership to the notification list, while section 6802(a) of the Intelligence Authorization Act amended the section generally, standing up the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office proper. The Senate-side drive came from SASC members, principally Senator Kirsten Gillibrand working with Senator Marco Rubio.

What the rewritten section actually demands is the interesting part. AARO's duties include developing procedures to synchronize and standardize the collection, reporting and analysis of UAP incidents, including adverse physiological effects, across the entire Department of Defense and intelligence community. The Secretary of Defense and the Director of National Intelligence must jointly designate an official responsible for ensuring the expertise, authorities, accesses, data, systems, platforms and capabilities exist for rapid response to and support for field investigations, and must designate one or more line organizations primarily responsible for scientific, technical and operational analysis of data, including with respect to the testing of materials, medical studies, and development of theoretical models. Congress wrote materials testing and medical studies into the statute. It also required that each designated line organization have authority to draw on the special expertise of persons outside the federal government with appropriate security clearances, and it listed the Department of Energy among the elements that may detail personnel to be physically located at the office.

The historical record report in subsection (j) is the closest thing to a congressional charge sheet in U.S. law. It requires a written report to the defense committees, the intelligence committees and congressional leadership covering the period beginning January 1, 1945, compiling the key historical record of intelligence community involvement with UAP, and specifically itemizing three things: any restricted-access program or activity not explicitly and clearly reported to Congress; successful or unsuccessful efforts to identify and track UAP; and any efforts to obfuscate, manipulate public opinion, hide, or otherwise provide incorrect information, classified or unclassified. The Archivist of the United States is directed to make NARA holdings, including classified holdings, available to AARO for that purpose. Congress then attached an auditor: section 6803 of Public Law 117-263 required the Comptroller General to identify cleared GAO personnel to audit the historical record report process, to conduct work on site as appropriate, and to brief the intelligence committees, the defense committees and congressional leadership semiannually on AARO's progress and its compliance with legislative requirements. That requirement was extended by Public Law 118-159 section 6802 in December 2024.

The FY2024 NDAA added the money lever. Section 1687(b) of Public Law 118-31 made independent research and development funding relating to UAP unallowable as an indirect expense on contracts covered by DoD Instruction 3204.01 unless the material is made available to the congressional defense committees, both intelligence committees, and the majority and minority leaders of the Senate and the Speaker and minority leader of the House. This is the appropriations-side answer to the classification-side problem, and its existence implies a belief that contractors were recovering UAP-related costs through overhead.

The FY2026 NDAA, Public Law 119-60, enacted December 18, 2025, shows what still was not working. Section 1671 added a new subsection (l)(5) requiring every semiannual briefing to include details on any UAP intercepts conducted by the North American Aerospace Defense Command or United States Northern Command, including the number, location and nature of the intercepts and a description of the procedures and protocols followed, including any data collected or analyzed during such intercepts, and requiring the AARO Director to inform Congress of any failure by NORAD or NORTHCOM to provide timely information. Section 1671(b) reached backward, requiring the first briefing after enactment to cover intercepts not previously reported going back to January 1, 2004. Section 1673(a) gave the AARO Director 180 days to produce an accounting of the security classification guides that apply to information used for UAP reports and investigations, with discretionary authority to issue a consolidated security classification matrix. Section 1672(b) rewrote the data-availability clause so that the immediate-production requirement now binds each element of the intelligence community and component of the Department of Defense with UAP data, where the prior text bound only intelligence community elements.

That last amendment is the single most damning line in the sequence. From December 2022 to December 2025, the statutory command to hand UAP data over immediately did not reach Department of Defense components as such. The department that operates the special access program system, that houses DoD SAPCO, and that owns the classification guides sat outside the mandate for three years, and it took an act of Congress in December 2025 to close it.

What SASC has not delivered is the enforcement architecture. The UAP Disclosure Act, offered by Senators Chuck Schumer and Mike Rounds as an NDAA amendment and modeled on the JFK Assassination Records Collection Act, would have created a nine-member presidentially appointed civilian Review Board with subpoena power and would have asserted federal eminent domain over recovered technologies of unknown origin held by private entities. The Review Board and the eminent domain provision were stripped in conference in FY2024, and the Act was excluded again from the FY2026 NDAA. What survived was a records collection with no independent adjudicator. The one provision that would have reached into contractor custody, eminent domain over recovered technologies of unknown origin, is the one that has never made it into law.

claims.text: 10 U.S.C. 119(g)(1) names the Committee on Armed Services of the Senate as one of the 'defense committees' entitled to special access program notification, making its chairman and ranking minority member two of the eight members who may be advised of a waived SAP under section 119(e)(2).

The statutory basis for AARO originates in section 1683 of the FY2022 NDAA, Public Law 117-81, division A, title XVI, December 27, 2021, 135 Stat. 2118, and was amended generally by Public Law 117-263 section 1673(c) and Intelligence Authorization Act section 6802(a) on December 23, 2022.

50 U.S.C. 3373(j)(1)(B)(ii)(I) requires AARO's historical record report to include 'any program or activity that was protected by restricted access that has not been explicitly and clearly reported to Congress.'

50 U.S.C. 3373(j)(1)(B)(ii)(III) requires the report to include 'any efforts to obfuscate, manipulate public opinion, hide, or otherwise provide incorrect unclassified or classified information about unidentified anomalous phenomena or related activities.'

50 U.S.C. 3373(l)(4) requires the AARO Director to provide to the chair and ranking member of the Senate and House Armed Services Committees and the congressional intelligence committees 'an enumeration of any instances in which data relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena was not provided to the Office because of classification restrictions on that data or for any other reason.'

Section 1672(b) of the FY2026 NDAA, Public Law 119-60 (December 18, 2025, 139 Stat. 1202), amended 50 U.S.C. 3373(f)(1)(A) to require that 'each element of the intelligence community and component of the Department of Defense' with UAP data make it immediately available to AARO; the prior text bound only intelligence community elements.

Section 1671(a) of Public Law 119-60 added 50 U.S.C. 3373(l)(5), requiring each semiannual briefing to detail any UAP intercepts conducted by NORAD or U.S. Northern Command, including 'the number, location, and nature of such intercepts' and 'a description of the procedures and protocols followed during the intercepts, including any data collected or analyzed during such intercepts', and requiring notice to Congress of any failure by NORAD or NORTHCOM to provide timely information.
Section 1671(b) of Public Law 119-60 requires the first post-enactment briefing to include previously unreported NORAD and NORTHCOM UAP intercepts occurring from January 1, 2004 onward.

Section 1673(a) of Public Law 119-60 requires the AARO Director, within 180 days of December 18, 2025, to make an accounting of security classification guides that apply to information used for UAP reports and investigations, and permits issuance of a consolidated security classification matrix for UAP-related programs.

50 U.S.C. 3373(e) requires designation of one or more line organizations primarily responsible for scientific, technical and operational analysis of UAP data 'including with respect to the testing of materials, medical studies, and development of theoretical models', and requires that each such organization have authority to draw on the special expertise of persons outside the federal government with appropriate security clearances.

50 U.S.C. 3373(i) lists the Department of Energy among the elements that may provide detailees to be physically located at AARO, alongside CIA, DIA, NSA, NGA, the service intelligence elements and DHS.

Section 6803 of Public Law 117-263 required the Comptroller General to identify cleared GAO personnel to audit the AARO historical record report process, including on-site work, and to brief the intelligence committees, defense committees and congressional leadership semiannually on AARO's progress and compliance with legislative requirements; the requirement was extended by Public Law 118-159 section 6802 (December 23, 2024).

Section 1687(b) of the FY2024 NDAA, Public Law 118-31 (137 Stat. 621), bars UAP-related independent research and development funding from being allowable as an indirect expense on contracts covered by DoD Instruction 3204.01 unless the material is made available to the congressional defense committees, HPSCI, SSCI and the four congressional leaders.

The UAP Disclosure Act, offered by Senators Chuck Schumer and Mike Rounds as an amendment to the FY2024 NDAA and modeled on the JFK Assassination Records Collection Act, would have created a nine-member civilian Review Board empowered to hold hearings, administer oaths and subpoena witnesses and documents, and would have asserted eminent domain over recovered technologies of unknown origin held by private entities; the Review Board and eminent domain provisions were stripped in conference and the Act was again excluded from the FY2026 NDAA.
